Key Message 1...Cool weather and periodic showers and 
thunderstorms, some of the lake-effect variety, are expected 
through Tuesday.

Aloft, a low should wobble ENE'ward from the northern Great
Lakes to near the Gulf of St. Lawrence the rest of today through
Tuesday. In response, cyclonic flow, initially SW'erly to 
W'erly over our region, veers to NW'erly overnight tonight into
Monday and then remains NW'erly through Tuesday. Shortwave 
disturbances embedded in the cyclonic flow will continue to 
impact Western and Central NY. At the surface, a cold front was 
located near I-81 at 1:35 PM EDT. This front will continue 
moving E'ward and should exit the rest of our CWA by 4 PM at the
latest. Behind the front, a lake-aggregate trough is expected 
to persist through Monday night and then a high pressure ridge 
will begin to build from the western and central Great Lakes on 
Tuesday. Net low-level CAA will impact our region behind the 
cold front. Accordingly, late afternoon highs should reach the 
mid 60's to mid 70's today and Tuesday, respectively. In 
between, Monday is expected to feature highs only in the 60's to
lower 70's courtesy of colder 850 mb temperatures and rather 
abundant cloud cover, including diurnal cumuliform clouds. 
Overnight lows should reach mainly the upper 40's to upper 50's 
around daybreak Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday, respectively.

Outside lake-effect precip (details below), isolated to 
scattered showers and thunderstorms are expected the rest of 
today through Monday night as low-level convergence/moist ascent
along the cold front and surface trough axes accompanying the 
shortwave disturbances release at least weak potential 
instability in the lowest ~1 km AGL and weak boundary layer CAPE
stemming from daytime warming through this early evening and 
again late Monday morning through early evening. Behind the cold
front, scattered lake-effect rain showers and thunderstorms 
have already developed over/downwind of Lake Erie and over much 
of Lake Ontario. Lake-effect rain showers and thunderstorms with
periods of heavy rainfall will continue through Monday night as
synoptic-scale low-level moisture remains deep/abundant and 850
mb temperatures around 8C to 10C continue to become established
over/downwind of ~23C to ~24C Lakes Erie and Ontario, behind 
the cold front. Those factors will yield sizable lake-induced 
CAPE and lake-induced EL's around 20kft to perhaps 30kft above 
lake level. 

The passage of the aforementioned shortwave troughs will cause 
mean low-level flow direction to vary over and downwind of Lakes
Erie and Ontario. Accordingly, lake-effect precip should 
primarily stream ESE'ward or SE'ward from Lake Erie through 
Monday night. However, a period of W'erly to WSW'erly mean low-level
flow should allow lake-effect precip to stream E'ward or
ENE'ward from the lake during most of the predawn and daylight 
hours of Monday. This lake-effect precip should remain south of
Buffalo. As for Lake Ontario, mean low-level flow should allow 
lake-effect precip to impact locations generally northeast of 
the lake through Monday afternoon, before the precip shifts 
S'ward and eventually settles southeast of the lake Monday 
evening through Monday night as a shortwave trough axis passage 
causes mean low-level flow to veer from SW'erly to NW'erly 
over/downwind of the lake. Note: lake-effect precip is expected
to be most-organized tonight into Monday morning and again 
Monday night into Tuesday morning, when nocturnal cooling will 
allow Lakes Erie and Ontario to be the primary sources of 
warmth, moisture, and instability. 

On Tuesday, lake-effect rain showers and thunderstorms are
expected to stream generally SE'ward from Lakes Erie and
Ontario, but decrease in coverage/intensity and end by 
nightfall as the building surface ridge is accompanied by 
synoptic-scale low-level dry air advection, a lowering 
subsidence inversion, and increase in directional low-level 
vertical wind shear, which will all act to decrease lake-induced
CAPE. Primarily dry weather is expected outside the lake-effect
precip, but a few showers may accompany the passage of 
additional shortwave troughs/attendant surface trough axes 
coinciding with weak potential instability in the lowest ~1 km 
AGL. 

Key Message 2...Dry weather expected region-wide this Tuesday night 
through Wednesday.

The high pressure ridge at the surface and aloft will build from
the central Great Lakes Tuesday night and then begin to exit
toward New England on Wednesday. Dry weather is expected as
stabilizing subsidence accompanies the ridge. Considerable
clearing, low humidity, and weak surface winds should allow lows
to reach mainly the mid 40's to mid 50's around daybreak
Wednesday. Mainly clear to party cloudy sky and net low-level
WAA along the western flank of the surface ridge should allow
highs to rebound to mainly the mid 70's to lower 80's late
Wednesday afternoon.
